anton-rubinstein.story: Rubinstein was a star pianist before he was a staple here. In 1872–73 he gave 215 American concerts in 239 days, “sometimes two and three a day,” and wrote afterwards, “May Heaven preserve us from such slavery!” Theodore Thomas’s orchestra played with him in New York, and Thomas, later the Philharmonic’s music director, kept his music on its programs. After Rubinstein died in 1894 it slowly lost its place.
anton-rubinstein.short: Theodore Thomas led 12 of his 13 performances in the 1880s; a slow fade after that.
anton-rubinstein.text: Theodore Thomas led 12 of his 13 performances in the 1880s, but others kept playing him after that. He faded over decades, not at one moment; the sparkline shows the slope.

henry-kimball-hadley.story: In 1921 Hadley became the Philharmonic’s associate conductor, the first American to hold a full-time post with a major American orchestra. Mahler had conducted his rhapsody The Culprit Fay here in 1911; in the 1920s Hadley took it on tour himself, again and again. In 1926 Warner Brothers had him conduct the orchestra at the New York premiere of John Barrymore’s Don Juan. He resigned in 1927, and his music left with him.
henry-kimball-hadley.short: He conducted 96 of his own 109 performances in the 1920s; then 10 in the ten seasons after he stopped; Culprit Fay Rhapsody, Op. 62 was 57 of the 109.
henry-kimball-hadley.text: He mostly conducted his own music: 96 of his 109 performances in the 1920s were under his own baton. After he last conducted his music, in 1932-33, everyone else together played him 10 times in the next ten seasons. One piece carried him: Culprit Fay Rhapsody, Op. 62, 57 of the 109.
henry-kimball-hadley.note: Hadley was the Philharmonic’s associate conductor from 1921 to 1927, the first American to hold a full-time post with a major American orchestra.

william-schuman.story: Schuman was a New York institution: president of Juilliard from 1945, then of Lincoln Center, the Philharmonic’s new home, from 1961 to 1969. He and Leonard Bernstein were close; on the TV panel show What’s My Line?, asked if he was Bernstein, he answered, “I’m his friend.” In 1962 Bernstein and the orchestra premiered his Eighth Symphony and recorded it days later. His Philharmonic heyday was Bernstein’s.
william-schuman.short: Leonard Bernstein led 39 of his 84 performances in the 1960s; then 24 in the ten seasons after Bernstein stopped.
william-schuman.text: Leonard Bernstein, music director from 1958 to 1969, led 39 of his 84 performances in the 1960s. After Leonard Bernstein last led his music, in 1985-86, everyone else together played him 24 times in the next ten seasons.

karl-goldmark.story: Goldmark was one of Vienna’s leading composers and a friend of Brahms, who liked his Rustic Wedding Symphony. Wagner, a strong influence on him, kept his distance: Wagner’s antisemitism “stood in the way of any genuine warmth between them.” Josef Stransky, Mahler’s successor, played Goldmark more than anyone before or since. Goldmark died in Vienna in January 1915, in the middle of that run.
karl-goldmark.short: Josef Stransky led 46 of his 50 performances in the 1910s; then 18 in the ten seasons after Stransky stopped.
karl-goldmark.text: Josef Stransky, music director from 1911 to 1923, led 46 of his 50 performances in the 1910s. After Josef Stransky last led his music, in 1919-20, everyone else together played him 18 times in the next ten seasons.

mikhail-ippolitov-ivanov.story: Ippolitov-Ivanov spent seven years running the music academy and orchestra in Tiflis, Georgia, and the music he heard there became Caucasian Sketches. Its march, Procession of the Sardar, turned into a pops favorite, just the kind of piece the Philharmonic’s summer Stadium nights were built on. It is the only music of his the orchestra has played.
mikhail-ippolitov-ivanov.short: 24 of his 55 performances in the 1920s were summer Stadium concerts; a slow fade after that; Caucasian Sketches, Suite No. 1 was 55 of the 55.
mikhail-ippolitov-ivanov.text: 24 of his 55 performances in the 1920s were summer Stadium concerts, under 7 conductors. He faded over decades, not at one moment; the sparkline shows the slope. One piece carried him: Caucasian Sketches, Suite No. 1, 55 of the 55.

ernest-schelling.story: Schelling, a concert pianist, spent the First World War as an assistant American military attaché in Bern, Switzerland. His hit, A Victory Ball, sets Alfred Noyes’s poem in which young soldiers killed in the war watch a victory party that has already forgotten them; Mengelberg and the Philharmonic recorded it. From 1924 until his death in 1939 he was “Uncle Ernest,” founder of the orchestra’s Young People’s Concerts, and led 295 of them.
ernest-schelling.short: Willem Mengelberg led 28 of his 53 performances in the 1920s; then 21 in the ten seasons after Mengelberg stopped; A Victory Ball was 30 of the 53.
ernest-schelling.text: Willem Mengelberg, music director from 1922 to 1928, led 28 of his 53 performances in the 1920s. After Willem Mengelberg last led his music, in 1927-28, everyone else together played him 21 times in the next ten seasons. One piece carried him: A Victory Ball, 30 of the 53.
ernest-schelling.note: Schelling was the first conductor of the Philharmonic’s Young People’s Concerts, which began in March 1924.

frederick-delius.story: Delius had one great champion, Thomas Beecham, who took up his music in 1907 and never let it go. By the late 1920s Delius was blind and paralysed, finishing his last pieces with the help of a young assistant, Eric Fenby; he died in 1934. His New York moment came just then, with Beecham and with John Barbirolli, the Englishman who became the Philharmonic’s music director in 1936.
frederick-delius.short: John Barbirolli led 22 of his 48 performances in the 1930s; then 15 in the ten seasons after Barbirolli stopped.
frederick-delius.text: John Barbirolli, music director from 1936 to 1941, led 22 of his 48 performances in the 1930s. After John Barbirolli last led his music, in 1962-63, everyone else together played him 15 times in the next ten seasons.

jaromir-weinberger.story: In 1930 Weinberger’s Schwanda the Bagpiper was the most performed opera in German-language houses. Because he was Jewish, the Nazis banned it, and in 1939 he fled to America. On October 12 that year Barbirolli and the Philharmonic premiered his variations Under the Spreading Chestnut Tree, his only real success in exile. Worn down by illness, money worries and the neglect of his music, he took his own life in 1967.
sources: Wikipedia: Under the Spreading Chestnut Tree
jaromir-weinberger.short: John Barbirolli led 23 of his 39 performances in the 1930s; then 10 in the ten seasons after Barbirolli stopped; Schwanda the Bagpiper was 21 of the 39.
jaromir-weinberger.text: John Barbirolli, music director from 1936 to 1941, led 23 of his 39 performances in the 1930s. After John Barbirolli last led his music, in 1942-43, everyone else together played him 10 times in the next ten seasons. One piece carried him: Schwanda the Bagpiper, 21 of the 39.
jaromir-weinberger.note: Schwanda the Bagpiper was a hit on stages worldwide. Weinberger, born into a Jewish family in Prague, fled the Nazis for the US in 1939; none of his later works matched it.

hugo-wolf.story: Wolf was above all a song composer, and the Philharmonic mostly heard him through his songs arranged for orchestra. He spent his last years in a Vienna asylum and died there in 1903, aged 42, so in the 1910s his was a recently lost voice.
hugo-wolf.short: Josef Stransky led 9 of his 22 performances in the 1910s; then 3 in the ten seasons after Stransky stopped.
hugo-wolf.text: Josef Stransky, music director from 1911 to 1923, led 9 of his 22 performances in the 1910s. After Josef Stransky last led his music, in 1916-17, everyone else together played him 3 times in the next ten seasons.

rubin-goldmark.story: Rubin Goldmark was born in New York, a nephew of Karl Goldmark and a pupil of Dvořák. He is remembered as a teacher: a 15-year-old Aaron Copland studied with him and found him “too pedantic and academic,” and George Gershwin turned to him while writing the Concerto in F. He ran composition at Juilliard from 1924 until he died on March 6, 1936. Three weeks later the Philharmonic played his music for the last time.
rubin-goldmark.short: Willem Mengelberg led 21 of his 34 performances in the 1920s; then 9 in the ten seasons after Mengelberg stopped; A Negro Rhapsody was 24 of the 34.
rubin-goldmark.text: Willem Mengelberg, music director from 1922 to 1928, led 21 of his 34 performances in the 1920s. After Willem Mengelberg last led his music, in 1927-28, everyone else together played him 9 times in the next ten seasons. One piece carried him: A Negro Rhapsody, 24 of the 34.

george-whitefield-chadwick.story: Chadwick ran Boston’s New England Conservatory and taught a generation of American composers, Henry Hadley and Florence Price among them. Josef Stransky programmed more Americans than all his predecessors combined, and Chadwick was the first name on his list. The piece that stuck was Tam O’Shanter, a Robert Burns tale told in sound.
george-whitefield-chadwick.short: Josef Stransky led 17 of his 21 performances in the 1910s; then 5 in the ten seasons after Stransky stopped; Tam O’Shanter was 11 of the 21.
george-whitefield-chadwick.text: Josef Stransky, music director from 1911 to 1923, led 17 of his 21 performances in the 1910s. After Josef Stransky last led his music, in 1922-23, everyone else together played him 5 times in the next ten seasons. One piece carried him: Tam O’Shanter, 11 of the 21.

josef-stransky.story: Stransky got the top job in 1911 as Mahler’s successor, and one critic compared the appointment to Aesop’s mountain in labor that “brought forth a mouse.” From his own podium, his own music got played. After the Philharmonic merged with the National Symphony in 1921 and Willem Mengelberg arrived, Stransky left, and left music altogether: he became an art dealer, specializing in Picasso’s Rose Period.
josef-stransky.short: He conducted 21 of his own 21 performances in the 1910s; then 0 in the ten seasons after he stopped.
josef-stransky.text: He mostly conducted his own music: 21 of his 21 performances in the 1910s were under his own baton. After he last conducted his music, in 1920-21, nobody played him for ten seasons.

edward-a-macdowell.story: MacDowell was best known for short piano pieces like To a Wild Rose, and in 1907 he and his wife gave their farm in Peterborough, New Hampshire, to become the MacDowell Colony, a retreat for artists. He died the next year. His tuneful miniatures suited Ernest Schelling’s Young People’s Concerts, but over the century Ives, Copland and Harris took his place as the American composers people played.
edward-a-macdowell.short: Ernest Schelling led 16 of his 33 performances in the 1920s; then 12 in the ten seasons after Schelling stopped.
edward-a-macdowell.text: Ernest Schelling led 16 of his 33 performances in the 1920s. After Ernest Schelling last led his music, in 1936-37, everyone else together played him 12 times in the next ten seasons.

morton-gould.story: Gould came out of radio: by 1935 he was conducting and arranging for New York’s WOR, heard across the country, and his 1940s hits were radio music made for concert halls. He kept working for half a century, led ASCAP, and won the Pulitzer Prize in 1995 for Stringmusic, a year before he died. By then the Philharmonic had moved on.
morton-gould.short: 12 conductors shared his 37 performances in the 1940s; a slow fade after that.
morton-gould.text: No single champion: 12 conductors shared his 37 performances in the 1940s. He faded over decades, not at one moment; the sparkline shows the slope.

max-reger.story: Reger was a major figure in Germany, and Schoenberg called him a genius, but in New York he was Josef Stransky’s cause alone. He died of a heart attack in a Leipzig hotel in May 1916, and in wartime Stransky’s programs leaned toward English, Russian and French music. Once Stransky left, nobody picked Reger up.
max-reger.short: Josef Stransky led 29 of his 29 performances in the 1910s; then 9 in the ten seasons after Stransky stopped.
max-reger.text: Josef Stransky, music director from 1911 to 1923, led 29 of his 29 performances in the 1910s. After Josef Stransky last led his music, in 1922-23, everyone else together played him 9 times in the next ten seasons.

gustave-charpentier.story: Charpentier was really one work. His opera Louise was an immediate success in Paris in 1900 and reached its 500th performance at the Opéra-Comique in 1921. Its sequel, Julien, was “quickly forgotten” after a lukewarm 1913 premiere, and he wrote very little after that.
gustave-charpentier.short: Josef Stransky led 19 of his 19 performances in the 1910s; a slow fade after that; Louise was 16 of the 19.
gustave-charpentier.text: Josef Stransky led 19 of his 19 performances in the 1910s, but others kept playing him after that. He faded over decades, not at one moment; the sparkline shows the slope. One piece carried him: Louise, 16 of the 19.

sigmund-romberg.story: Romberg was Broadway’s operetta king, the composer of The Student Prince, The Desert Song and The New Moon, and from 1945 to 1948 he had his own NBC radio show. In the 1940s he came to Lewisohn Stadium in the summers to conduct his own songs. He died of a stroke in 1951, aged 64, and the Romberg nights ended with him.
sigmund-romberg.short: He conducted 32 of his own 38 performances in the 1940s; then 3 in the ten seasons after he stopped.
sigmund-romberg.text: He mostly conducted his own music: 32 of his 38 performances in the 1940s were under his own baton. After he last conducted his music, in 1950-51, everyone else together played him 3 times in the next ten seasons.
